Facial Aesthetics

CO2 Laser Skin Resurfacing: Benefits, Risks, and Recovery

Learn how CO2 laser resurfacing works, how treatment depth changes recovery, and which risks and preparation questions deserve attention.

August 25, 20263 min readPublished by The House of Dental

Resurfacing creates a controlled skin injury

A carbon dioxide laser delivers energy that removes very small areas of skin and heats surrounding tissue. The controlled injury starts a healing response that can soften the appearance of fine lines, sun damage, uneven texture, and some scars. It is a medical procedure, not a stronger version of a facial.

Ablative treatment removes surface tissue. Fractional treatment divides the beam into many narrow columns, leaving untreated skin between them. Fractional delivery can shorten recovery compared with fully ablative resurfacing, but device settings and treatment depth still make a large difference. The phrase CO2 laser does not describe one fixed experience.

The consultation should be specific

Skin type, the concern being treated, medical history, medications, past scarring, and previous pigment changes all influence the plan. A history of cold sores matters because laser treatment can reactivate the virus. Active infection, recent tanning, and some skin conditions may require postponement or a different approach.

Darker skin tones can be treated with lasers, but the risk of unwanted lightening or darkening needs careful evaluation. Provider experience, device choice, settings, and aftercare all matter. The consultation should include realistic improvement, likely downtime, alternatives, and the possibility that more than one treatment may be needed.

Recovery depends on depth

Redness, swelling, warmth, oozing, and peeling can occur after ablative resurfacing. The treated skin may need gentle cleansing, ointment, dressings, or other care specified by the provider. Healing may take several days or longer, and redness can persist after the surface has closed.

Sun protection is central before and after treatment because ultraviolet exposure can increase the risk of discoloration and interfere with healing. Makeup and active skin products should not be restarted until the provider says the skin barrier is ready. General timelines are useful for planning, but the written instructions for the actual device and settings are more reliable.

Know the risks before deciding

Possible complications include infection, prolonged redness, acne-like bumps, scarring, and pigment changes. People prone to cold sores may need preventive antiviral medication. Smoking and health conditions that affect healing should be discussed openly.

Call the treating clinician for worsening pain, spreading redness, pus, fever, clusters of blisters, or healing that does not follow the expected course. A careful plan balances the degree of improvement someone wants with the downtime and risk they are willing to accept.

CO2 is one option among several

Non-ablative lasers heat tissue without removing the surface in the same way, so recovery may be shorter and results more gradual. Erbium lasers, chemical peels, microneedling, and other procedures address overlapping concerns with different tradeoffs. No device is automatically best for every kind of scar, pigment change, or texture concern.

Ask why a specific laser and depth fit the concern, what the provider expects one session to change, and which alternatives carry less downtime. Treatment settings should follow an examination of the skin rather than a standard package chosen from a menu.

Photographs taken in consistent lighting can help document change over time, but they should not replace a skin examination or be treated as a guarantee. Lighting, makeup, camera processing, and healing stage can make casual before-and-after comparisons unreliable.

Sources and further reading

  1. American Society for Dermatologic Surgery: Laser Resurfacing
  2. American Academy of Dermatology: Questions Before Cosmetic Treatment
